doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Church, the depression and what makes jazz musicians happy
summary: Preachers addressed people's own conduct until activist ministers arrived; jazz thrived in the depression. Delta blues sang of sex and love, not injustice.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: So was the preacher’s message instead of asking God to change the stock market or change the white person, was it more directed at the people themselves that he was talking to and for them to do right by themselves?

Exactly. That’s what I got in church. Until the day of the activist minister, you know such as Martin Luther King and people like that, where they join in with the Civil Rights Movement, and they began to use the church and so forth, and they just completely went on against the thing and got away with it in the United States. The United States got away from the basic doctrine — the separation of church and state. It’s supposed to be something basic to America, why these people came over here, to separate the church from the state. But nobody ever thinks of that you know, because they’re so busy making special rules when they deal with the so-called black idiom in the United States. They just go off and they’ve got piles of stuff all over, and it’s nothing. It’s not worth their time. So I was making a correlation between what these guys are doing you know? How do you make a jazz musician happy? By introducing him to some good looking girls at a party, and some whiskey if he likes it, or some other thing if he likes that. That’s what makes a jazz musician happy. So they play just as well, some of the best jazz we have is during the depression.

People seem to really value their entertainment even more during the depression, is that a fair statement? That even if they didn’t have money to spend that they would really try their hardest to still get their entertainment?

Yeah. Well they hadn’t had that much money anyway. When did they have a lot of money? You know what I mean? They didn’t have any money during slavery, right? The reconstruction was a rough time. Some people got rich but not many. I mean there was a lot of sharecropping and so forth and all, there is even peonage, stuff like that approaching it. In Mississippi for example, where all along the Delta and so forth, which gave rise to a style of the blues. It’s very popular among New England college people and so forth, but I don’t think they were doing the same thing. I mean they weren’t even singing about freedom in the penitentiary. They were singing about sex and love and how they’re being double crossed because they’re in there, and they’re singing about the man being mean, but it’s basically because he’s keeping him away from his girl, it seems to me. Then somebody could come, you could cajole somebody into it, but even if they did things which was news, in response to the news, like a flood of the Mississippi or something like that, it still wasn’t about injustice or discrimination and stuff like that.
